```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

Every parse returns a `gender` code (`M`, `F` or `U`) and a
`gender_confidence`. Both are estimates from how often the given names are
recorded for men and for women in U.S. Census name lists. This article shows
how the score is computed, what the confidence means, when the parser falls
back to a default, and where the census table comes from.

The examples parse a few names with `parse_names()` and show the columns that matter here as a table:

```{r}
library(peopleparser)

show <- function(x, cols = c("salutation", "first_name", "middle_name",
                             "suffix", "gender", "gender_confidence")) {
  parse_names(x)[c("name", cols)] |> knitr::kable()
}
```

## The score

`determine_gender()` takes the census rows for the given-name tokens (the
first name and any middle names, never the surname), adds up their male and
female counts, and reports the larger side:

$$
\text{confidence} = 100 \times \frac{\max(n_{male},\, n_{female})}{n_{male} + n_{female}}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

```{r}
cd <- get_census_data(c("LESLIE"))
cd[, c("name", "male_value", "female_value")] |> knitr::kable()
determine_gender(cd)
```

The confidence is the share of people with these names who have the reported
gender. It runs from 50 (an even split) to 100 (only one gender recorded). It
is not the probability that this particular person has that gender, which
also depends on their age and on the population the record comes from.

```{r}
show(c("JOHN SMITH", "MARY SMITH", "LESLIE SMITH", "PAT SMITH",
       "CHRIS JONES", "TAYLOR SWIFT"))
```

Most first names in the table are strongly gendered. Of the
`r sum(census.names$first_name_value > 0)` first names, the majority gender
holds 95% or more of the count for most of them:

```{r}
fn <- census.names[census.names$first_name_value > 0, ]
share <- pmax(fn$male_value, fn$female_value) / (fn$male_value + fn$female_value)
table(cut(share, c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1), include.lowest = TRUE,
          labels = c("50-80%", "80-95%", "95-100%")))
```

### Middle names count too

The counts of all given-name tokens are pooled, so the middle name can move
the score. Because the counts are pooled rather than averaged, a very common
name outweighs a rare one, and two names of opposite gender give a weak score
whatever their order:

```{r}
show(c("SARAH MAY WILSON", "JOHN MARY SMITH", "MARY JOHN SMITH"))
```

## When there is no evidence

When no given-name token is in the census (an initial, a rare name, or no
given name at all), the parser falls back:

| Situation | `gender` | `gender_confidence` |
|-----------|----------|---------------------|
| given names not in the census, no suffix | `U` | `50.0` |
| given names not in the census, with `JR`, `SR`, `II`, ... | `M` | `50.0` |
| nothing left to parse | `U` | `0.0` |

The suffix rule reflects that generational suffixes are almost always used by
men. The 50.0 says that the call is a default, not evidence.

```{r}
show(c("J SMITH", "J SMITH JR", "A J SMITH", "TSHEPO CHO", "SMITH JR"))
```

## Salutations

`parse_name()` does not use the salutation for gender: `MR PAT SMITH` is
scored from `PAT` alone. If you need a salutation to override the census
score, do it after parsing:

```{r}
d <- parse_names(c("MR PAT SMITH", "MRS PAT SMITH", "DR PAT SMITH"))
d$gender_sal <- ifelse(d$salutation == "MR", "M",
                ifelse(d$salutation %in% c("MRS", "MS", "MISS"), "F", d$gender))
d[c("name", "salutation", "gender", "gender_confidence", "gender_sal")] |> knitr::kable()
```

The nickname functions do this already: in `nickname_lookup()` a gendered
salutation (`MR`, `MRS`, `MS`, `MISS`) beats the census score. See
`vignette("canonical-first-names")`.

## Using the scores

`gender_confidence` is returned as text. Convert it before comparing:

```{r}
d <- parse_names(c("JOHN SMITH", "PAT SMITH", "J SMITH", "CHRIS JONES"))
d$gender_confidence <- as.numeric(d$gender_confidence)
d$gender_80 <- ifelse(d$gender_confidence >= 80, d$gender, "U")
d[c("name", "gender", "gender_confidence", "gender_80")] |> knitr::kable()
```

A threshold of 80 (what `nickname_lookup()` uses) keeps most names and drops
the ones that are close to even. For counts of women and men in a population,
summing the shares can be better than counting hard calls, because it does
not round every `PAT` to female.

Keep in mind:

* The counts are for the whole U.S. population in 2020, children included.
  Name use changes over time (`LESLIE` and `ASHLEY` were once mostly male
  names; `TAYLOR` and `RILEY` have become mostly female) and across countries,
  so the score fits some groups better than others.
* The census lists record only male and female. The scores say nothing about
  how people identify.
* Names missing from the list, many of them non-English given names, get no
  score at all.

## Where the census table comes from

`census.names` is bundled with the package in `data/census.names.rda`. It is
not downloaded when the package is installed or used. It is built by
`data-raw/census_names.R` from the Census Bureau's 2020 name release,
*Frequently Occurring First Names and Last Names from the 2020 Census*
(revised April 2026):

```{r}
cn <- census.names
c(rows           = nrow(cn),
  male_names     = sum(cn$male_value > 0),
  female_names   = sum(cn$female_value > 0),
  first_names    = sum(cn$first_name_value > 0),
  surnames       = sum(cn$last_name_value > 0))
cn[cn$name %in% c("SMITH", "ALL OTHER NAMES"), ] |> knitr::kable()
```

* **Given names and gender:** every first name held by 91 or more people in
  the 2020 Census, with the count of people recorded male and female.
  `first_name_value` is `male_value + female_value`.
* **Surnames:** every surname held by 92 or more people, plus a catch-all
  `ALL OTHER NAMES` row (which no single name token matches).

**Earlier table.** Until November 2026 the package shipped a table built from
the 1990 first-name lists (1,219 male and 4,275 female names, published as
percentages and scaled to counts) and the 2010 surname file. The 2020 lists
hold ten times as many given names, so far fewer names get no gender. On a
sample of 9,608 Form 990 Part VII names, the 2020 table:

* matched the gender implied by an `MR`, `MRS` or `MS` salutation in 86% of
  cases, against 79%;
* left 227 names with unknown gender, against 727;
* kept the written first word as the first name in 96.3% of plain two- and
  three-word names, against 95.4%.

**Refreshing the table.** When the Bureau publishes new lists, update the file
names in `data-raw/census_names.R` and run it from the package root. It
downloads the files, records their sizes and SHA-256 hashes in
`data-raw/census-names-src.csv`, rebuilds the five columns, and prints a
comparison with the bundled table: size, names whose main role (first name
or surname) changes, and names whose majority gender flips. Set
`CENSUS_NAMES_SAVE=TRUE` to overwrite the bundled table, then rerun the tests
and compare parses before and after, since any change moves name-order and
gender results.
